items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN PHARMACY: APPLICATIONS, OPPORTUNITIES AND CHALLENGES
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping every stage of the medicine life cycle, from the identification of drug targets to the counselling of patients at the pharmacy counter. This review examines how AI technologies, chiefly machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing and generative models, are applied across pharmaceutical science and pharmacy practice, and weighs the opportunities they offer against the challenges that limit their safe adoption. In drug discovery, AI supports target identification, protein structure prediction, virtual screening, de novo molecular design, retrosynthesis, drug repurposing and clinical trial optimisation. In pharmaceutics and manufacturing, it is used to predict formulation behaviour, guide three-dimensional printing of dosage forms and enable real-time process control. In clinical, hospital and community pharmacy, AI-enabled tools assist prescription verification, prevention of adverse drug events, dose individualisation, adherence support, inventory management and patient communication. AI also strengthens pharmacovigilance, regulatory science and pharmacy education. The principal opportunities are shorter development timelines, lower attrition, personalised therapy, safer medication use and more efficient operations. The principal challenges are poor data quality and bias, limited transparency of complex models, privacy, unclear accountability, evolving regulation, validation gaps, fabricated output from language models and the need to prepare the pharmacy workforce. We conclude that AI is best viewed as a decision-support partner that extends, and does not replace, the professional judgement of pharmacists and pharmaceutical scientists, and we outline priorities for responsible implementation. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; Machine learning; Deep learning; Drug discovery; Pharmacy practice; Pharmacovigilance; Personalised medicine; Pharmaceutical manufacturing.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Diagnosis and Treatment of ADHD: Opportunities, Evidence, and Challenges
items.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental condition whose diagnosis still rests on clinical interviews and rating scales, and whose treatment is limited by partial response to medication, side effects, and unequal access to behavioural care. Artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning (ML) in particular, has been proposed as a way to make diagnosis more objective and treatment more personalised and scalable. This review summarises the current state of that evidence. In diagnosis, ML models trained on neuroimaging, electroencephalography (EEG), and behavioural or sensor data frequently report high accuracy, but results vary widely across datasets, are rarely validated externally, and have not yet produced a tool that clinicians can rely on. In treatment, the strongest evidence concerns a prescription digital therapeutic delivered as a video game-like intervention, whereas computerised cognitive training and neurofeedback show limited effects on blinded measures of ADHD symptoms. Key barriers are non-representative training data, algorithmic bias, privacy, weak regulatory and reporting standards, and the risk that predictive accuracy is mistaken for clinical utility. We conclude that AI is best positioned as decision support within a clinician-led, hybrid model of care, and we outline the research needed to move from promising prototypes to validated practice.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Pharmaceutical Industry: Transformative Applications, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: The pharmaceutical sector is dealing with a number of issues, such as growing R&D expenses, protracted drug development schedules, complicated regulations, supply chain interruptions, and heightened rivalry in the market. The development of new drugs is very resource intensive and often requires years of effort and billions of dollars as well as a high rate of clinical trial failures. The stringent regulatory requirements that demand extensive data validation and compliance further prolong the market entry process. There are also major issues related to counterfeit drugs and poor supply chain practice that are threats to both the business and the public. Artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the answers that can solve these problems with a change. AI-powered drug discovery cuts down on the time and expense involved with conventional methods by speeding up the identification of possible molecules. Machine learning algorithms can also help inform clinical trial designs and improve rates of successful trials by selecting the right patient population and predicting outcomes. AI-powered automation enhances compliance with regulations and ensures all documents are accurate and up to standard. AI can also help to predict demand, detect irregularities, and optimize logistics, minimizing the risk of shortages and counterfeit goods in manufacturing and supply chain management. Additionally, AI-powered personalized medicine reduces side effects and increases therapeutic efficacy by customizing therapies for each patient. Adoption of AI is hampered by issues including data protection, compatibility with existing systems, and governmental approval, despite its potential. With further advancements in AI, however, the pharmaceutical industry could benefit from increased involvement in addressing challenges, leading to improved patient outcomes, more efficient drug development, and better operational efficiency.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Clinical Decision Support Systems for Emergency Department Triage and Acute Care Prioritization: A Systematic Review of Accuracy, Safety, and Implementation Readiness
items.abstract: Background:AI is being increasingly investigated as a clinical decision support tool for ED triage and acute-care prioritization. Machine-learning, deep-learning, natural language processing (NLP) and large language model systems have shown good predictive performance but concerns remain about under-triage, over-triage, generalizability, workflow integration and implementation safety. We systematically reviewed the accuracy, safety and implementation readiness of AI-driven clinical decision-support systems for ED triage.Methods:This review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 recommendations. PubMed/MEDLINE, PubMed Central, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science and Cochrane Library were searched (citation chaining, reference-list screening and recent systematic reviews were also used). Of the 1076 records identified, 312 duplicates were removed and 764 records screened; 79 full-text reports were assessed and 65 excluded; fourteen studies were included in narrative synthesis. Meta-analysis was not performed because populations, AI architectures, triage systems, reference standards and outcome metrics are highly heterogeneous.Results:Conventional machine learning, gradient boosting, neural networks, deep learning, natural language processing and large language models were included in the studies. AI systems generally outperformed conventional triage for critical illness prediction (hospitalization), intensive-care admission and mortality; reported AUROCs for early mortality were 0.962 and for 30-day mortality 0.925. Direct triage systems also had some success: KATE had 75.7% ESI assignment accuracy; prospective GPT-4 and GPT-4o studieshad κ = 0.899 and multicenter κ = 0.833 with F1 = 0.897 agreement with expert triage but safety outcomes under-triage/over-triage subgroup performance and patient-important outcomes were inconsistently reported.Conclusions:ED triage systems powered by AI have great potential as supervised clinical decision support tools but not yet enough evidence to justify autonomous deployment. Prospective multicenter validation, standardized safety metrics, subgroup analysis, workflow evaluation, governance and post-deployment monitoring are needed before widespread implementation

items.abstract: Description / Abstract Title: Safeguarding Trust in AI-Assisted Credit Scoring in Indian Digital Lending: A Documentary Analysis of the RBI’s 2025 Directions Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and alternative data increasingly inform digital credit decisions, raising critical questions about privacy, fairness, decision transparency, and accountability. In India, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued the Digital Lending Directions, 2025 on 8 May 2025. This study examines these Directions as a dated regulatory instrument and assesses their coverage of trust-related safeguards. Reviewing the 2025 framework alongside earlier Indian digital-lending instruments, the study applies a five-part analytical framework developed from the literature: decision transparency, privacy and data minimisation, fairness, human recourse, and model governance. It also compares the Indian framework with international guidance from the European Banking Authority (EBA, 2020), the OECD (2021), and the US NIST (2023). The documentary analysis reveals that while the RBI framework provides robust coverage of lender conduct, data consent, disclosures (such as the Key Facts Statement with all-in APR), and grievance redress, it exhibits notable gaps regarding mandatory pre-deployment fairness testing, ongoing model-drift monitoring, and standardised explanations for AI-assisted adverse decisions. To bridge these gaps, the study proposes a layered set of safeguards: privacy-by-design, standardised reason codes for adverse decisions, accessible routes to human review, and periodic fairness and drift audits.

items.title: Artificial Stone Silicosis: New Face of an Old Disease
items.abstract: Artificial stone (AS) silicosis has emerged as a major global occupational health concern, challenging the perception of silicosis as a disease of the past. Driven by the fabrication of AS products containing high concentrations of crystalline silica (>90%), this rapidly progressive form disproportionately affects younger workers and develops after a much shorter exposure duration (median 7-19 years) than in classic silicosis. As cases continue to emerge worldwide, clinicians and occupational health practitioners are increasingly likely to encounter affected workers in clinical practice. This review provides a clinically focused synthesis of the current evidence on the epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, and management of AS silicosis. Compared with traditional silicosis, the unique physicochemical properties of AS dust may amplify lung toxicity and promote a self-perpetuating inflammatory response. This frequently results in rapid development of progressive massive fibrosis, with disease progression often continuing after exposure cessation. Diagnosis is often delayed because of overlapping clinical features and the limited sensitivity of conventional screening tools, highlighting the importance of early clinical recognition, detailed occupational history-taking, and the use of high-resolution computed tomography where appropriate. Lung transplantation remains the only definitive treatment for advanced disease, underscoring the importance of prevention. Effective prevention requires strong workplace controls, systematic medical surveillance, and appropriate regulatory measures. Clinicians play a key role in early detection, patient education, and mandatory disease reporting. Coordinated action across clinical, occupational, and policy domains is essential to improve recognition, strengthen preventive measures, and avert further cases of this highly preventable occupational disease.

items.title: Assistant or Ghostwriter? EAP Instructors’ Views on the Opportunities and Risks of GenAI in L2 Writing
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) systems are able to generate, revise and comment on second language (L2) student writing. However, less is known about where L2 writing teachers locate the opportunities and risks of such systems across the writing process. To that end, this study examined how English for academic purposes (EAP) writing instructors at two universities in Oman position GenAI within the L2 writing process. It focused on, first, the stages at which instructors locate GenAI's opportunities and risks, second, their views on GenAI as a source of feedback, and lastly their preparedness to manage academic integrity in AI-assisted L2 writing. A cross-sectional questionnaire combining Likert-scale items and open-ended prompts was completed by 51 EAP instructors , of whom 49 were retained for analysis. Closed items were analysed with descriptive statistics, Spearman correlations, McNemar tests and Mann–Whitney U tests. Open-ended responses were coded by writing stage through qualitative content analysis. The results showed that L2 writing instructors located GenAI's opportunities mainly in their own preparation of materials and model texts and in feedback. On the other hand, they highlighted its risks in students' drafting and in assessment. Revising and editing was contested, cited equally often as an opportunity and a risk. EAP instructors were more confident in using GenAI to prepare materials than in designing students' use of it at each writing stage. Just over half agreed that AI improves their feedback. This view was related to their overall attitude towards GenAI but not to their confidence as feedback providers. Most instructors felt responsible for checking students' GenAI use and confident in setting boundaries, but their confidence in maintaining academic integrity was unrelated to this sense of responsibility. More EAP instructors reported knowing how to use AI detectors than understanding how such detectors work. The study concludes that EAP instructors' readiness to integrate GenAI into L2 writing teaching and learning is uneven across the L2 writing process. Professional learning and development should therefore target the pedagogical design of student-facing AI use, the evaluation of AI feedback, AI detection literacy, and L2 writing assessment redesign.

items.abstract: In Brazil's 2026 presidential first round, the ballot box contradicted most polls: 136 of the 161 national polls showed Lula da Silva ahead, but Flávio Bolsonaro finished first. Public debate swung between fraud claims and the margin of error, and no open resource let students verify either with real data. Following a design and development approach, this study used generative AI (GenAI) under human curation to build the Atlas of the Errômetro, an open educational resource in which each section lets users learn, question, and test how registered polls compared with the official result. Data on 1,297 registrations came from the Superior Electoral Court, results were located through documentary search, and automated programs gathered report status and 130 compliance audits. The 901 included polls were compared with the ballot using the declared margin, the A index, the audit category, and a retrospective revealed-efficiency measure. Only 5.9% of the 896 comparable polls fell within their margin (31.5% in the last three days), against about 92% expected under unbiased random sampling; errors were systematic, with 530 nominally significant deviations toward Lula against 82 toward Flávio; Compliant or Caution polls erred less (7.1 versus 8.1 percentage points) but leaned toward Lula as often; and declared cost showed no detectable association with accuracy, with random-sample equivalence of about 2.3%. Each finding became an inquiry users can repeat, with activities, exam-style items, and games verified by automated tests. This first design cycle shows feasibility; effects on learning remain to be evaluated.

items.title: Attitudes and perceptions toward the use of artificial intelligence chatbots for peer review in medical journals: a large-scale, international cross-sectional survey
items.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence chatbots (AICs) are increasingly being considered for use in scholarly peer review to assist with tasks such as identifying methodological issues, verifying references, and improving language clarity. However, concerns remain regarding their reliability, ethical implications, and transparency. Evidence on how medical journal peer reviewers perceive the role and impact of AICs is limited. This study explored reviewers’ familiarity with AICs, perceived benefits and challenges, ethical concerns, and anticipated future roles in peer review. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional online survey of medical journal peer reviewers. Corresponding author information was extracted from MEDLINE-indexed articles added to PubMed within a six-week period. A total of 72,851 authors were invited via email to participate; those who self-identified as peer reviewers were eligible. The 29-item survey assessed familiarity with AICs and perceptions of their benefits and limitations in peer review. The survey was administered via SurveyMonkey from April 28 to June 16, 2025, with two reminder emails sent during the data collection period. Results Of 66,679 email invitations, a total of 1260 respondents provided survey responses (response rate: 1.9%), of whom 1157 met the eligibility criteria, and 1077 answered the main survey questions. Most participants were familiar with AICs (86.2%) and had used them for general purposes (87.7%), though most report not using AICs for peer review purposes (70.3%). Most respondents reported that their institutions do not provide training on AIC use in peer review (69.5%), although many expressed interest in such training (60.7%). Perceptions of AIC benefits were mixed, while concerns were widely shared, particularly regarding potential algorithmic bias (80.3%) and issues related to trust and user acceptance (73.3%). Conclusions While familiarity with AICs is high among medical journal peer reviewers, their reported use in peer review remains limited. There is clear interest in training and guidance, however, concerns related to ethics, data privacy, and research integrity persist and should be addressed before broader implementation.

items.title: Avoiding Cognitive Surrender in AI-Driven Ergonomics: A 27-Year Brazilian Perspective for the Global Market - From Reactive to Predictive
items.abstract: AbstractThis article explores the concept of Cognitive Surrender in AI-Driven Ergonomics — the risk that as AI becomes more competent in safety, human judgment is outsourced. Drawing on 27 years of EHS experience in Brazil (SP, GO, RJ, MS) managing Safety, Fire Protection and Road Safety in sugar-ethanol plants, soybean processing and construction, and now building EkoSeg EHS US LLC in Salt Lake City, UT, the author argues for AI for Augmentation, not Automation. The study bridges Brazil's NR-17 Ergonomic Work Analysis (AET) and OSHA's MSD prevention, analyzing the emergence of computer vision solutions like Kinebot (Curitiba), validated by Marfrig, P&G, Electrolux, with R$3M investment in Feb 2026 for global expansion. Kinebot delivers 5x faster and 80% cheaper analysis via phone video. The author presents lessons from the 62nd NISO Conference, Killarney, Ireland (2026): dashboards (Power BI integrating Safety Observations, NC, OFI, Near Miss, Training Expiry) don't save lives alone; conversations do. A framework is proposed: (a) Keep the Worker in the Loop — every AI high-risk flag (RULA 7) must trigger a Gemba walk, (b) Use Leading Indicators — % stations analyzed by AI, training validity, (c) Bridge NR-17 and OSHA. Author: Jailton da Silva, EHS Manager, 27 Years in HSE, Founder EkoSeg EHS US LLC & EkoSeg Segurança e Meio Ambiente, Brazil to Utah. Keywords: Cognitive Surrender, AI-Driven Ergonomics, NR-17, OSHA, RULA, REBA, Kinebot, EHS, Power BI, EkoSeg

items.title: AWARENESS AND PERCEPTION OF ROBO ADVISORY SERVICES AMONG INVESTORS IN MALAPPURAM
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology is changing the financial industry by providing inexpensive, automated, and customized tools to individual and institutional investors, revolutionising the way people make financial decisions. This study intends to evaluate the awareness and perception of robo-advisory services among investors in Malappuram district. Robo-advisors are computer-generated algorithms that provide Investment advice, Portfolio management, and financial planning solutions to customers without requiring much intervention from a human advisor by utilizing Artificial Intelligence and Data Analytics. This study also aims to study the perception of acceptance, its influencing factors, and the perception of investors towards acceptance of robo-advisory services. It was an integrated descriptive research design. Data was obtained from 120 investors made with the help of purposive sampling, using a structured online questionnaire. Data analysis was done using descriptive statistics, weighted mean analysis, and a one-sample test. The results show that the investors had a positive perception towards the use of robo-advisory, and the most preferred domain where robo-advisory services would be used was in Portfolio Management and Financial Planning. The overall mean perception score stood at 3.605 (where '3' is the neutral point) which was significantly more than the neutral point. The perception of investors in Malappuram was found to be favourable, thus indicating the potential for a higher penetration rate of robo-advisory services, also as increasing awareness and information, robust security systems, transparency, and user trust are essential for larger adoption.

items.title: Baby-schema-related cues shape moral expectations about decision-makers: evidence from names, faces, and AI avatars
items.abstract: People routinely form expectations about how others will behave in morally difficult situations, and such expectations guide consequential decisions, including whom to trust, hire, or delegate responsibility to. The present research examined whether baby-schema-related cues systematically bias these moral predictions. Across three experiments with Chinese university students (total N = 858), we tested three manifestations of baby-schema-related cues that share the function of evoking infant-like associations: repeated two-syllable names (Experiment 1), babyfaced appearance (Experiment 2), and visually cute artificial intelligence (AI) avatar designs (Experiment 3). Participants consistently perceived decision-makers displaying baby-schema-related cues as less likely to make utilitarian choices involving direct harm to others. The results show that superficially irrelevant social cues can bias moral expectations about others, although the underlying psychological mechanism remains to be clarified. These findings are relevant to moral psychology, person perception, and the design and evaluation of AI systems.

items.title: Balancing Innovation and Humanity: Advanced Practice Nurses Harnessing AI in Mental Health Care
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing mental health care through applications in screening, risk prediction, clinical decision support, documentation, and patient engagement. While these technologies improve efficiency and access, they also present ethical, clinical, and equity challenges that must be addressed in advanced practice nursing. This review synthesizes contemporary evidence on AI in mental health care and discusses its implications for advanced practice nurses (APNs), focusing on ethical implementation, equitable care, and policy. METHODS: An evidence-informed review of literature from 2019 to 2025 was conducted across various databases, including PubMed, CINAHL, and Google Scholar. The review covered AI applications, ethical considerations, health equity, and governance to identify themes relevant to APN practice. RESULTS: AI can enhance psychiatric assessments and patient engagement when used as a decision-support tool. However, challenges such as algorithmic bias, inconsistent performance, privacy concerns, and reliance on AI-generated recommendations persist. Emphasizing AI literacy, competency, and governance is crucial for safe, equitable implementation. CONCLUSION: APNs are well-suited to lead the ethical integration of AI in mental health care by merging evidence-based practice and patient advocacy. Ongoing investment in education, policy, and equitable governance is vital for maximizing AI's benefits while maintaining strong therapeutic relationships and quality care.

items.title: Barrier Verification and Leading-Indicator Governance for High-Risk Technical Operations in Oil and Gas and Construction Projects: An Integrative Review
items.abstract: High-risk technical operations in oil and gas facilities and construction projects remain difficult to control because work is temporary, interfaces are fragmented, hazardous energy is frequently introduced or released, and schedule pressure can weaken otherwise mature safety systems. This review examines how safety interventions can be configured so that engineered barriers, work-control verification, competence assurance, contractor governance and leading indicators operate as a connected assurance system rather than as isolated programs. A structured integrative review of peer-reviewed literature published from 2020 to 2025 was undertaken, with emphasis on construction safety, oil and gas safety climate, proactive indicators, digital work controls and sociotechnical risk management. The evidence shows that personal-safety programs are valuable for routine exposure reduction, but they do not by themselves provide credible assurance against low-frequency, high-consequence events. Stronger intervention logic emerges when the control selected is matched to the failure mode: physical barriers for hazardous energy, verified permits and isolations for temporary configuration change, competence controls for judgement-intensive tasks, disclosure mechanisms for weak signals, and governance controls for contractor and schedule interfaces. Leading indicators are most useful when they measure the condition of these controls rather than the volume of safety activity. The review develops an integrated assurance framework and proposes practical indicator families for project and operational settings. The central conclusion is that intervention quality depends less on the number of safety initiatives than on whether each critical control is owned, independently verifiable, time-sensitive and connected to decision authority before exposure escalates.

items.title: Barriers to Adopting AI-Driven Design Technologies in Architectural SMEs in Developing Countries: Evidence from a Delphi Survey in Iraq
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is entering architectural design through generative modelling and data-assisted decision support. In developing countries, most of this work is still carried out by architectural small and medium-sized enterprises with limited resources and uneven digital infrastructure. Existing studies have rarely examined how barriers to AI-driven design are ordered. This paper addresses that gap in Iraq. A literature list of 30 statements was refined by a 15-member Delphi panel into 22 barriers in five dimensions. The measurement model was assessed with partial least squares structural equation modelling on 83 practitioner responses. Interpretive structural modelling and MICMAC analysis then placed the dimensions in hierarchy, and the resulting paths were tested on the same data. Economic and institutional deficiencies occupy the driving level. Technological and data readiness acts as a linking layer, while human and organisational capacity and professional risk appear as dependent outcomes. All four paths were significant, the strongest running from institutional deficiencies to technological readiness. The findings indicate that economic and institutional conditions occupy the driving level in the expert hierarchy, while human capacity and professional risk appear as dependent outcomes. All four adjacent paths implied by that hierarchy were statistically significant in the survey data.

items.title: Becoming the Teacher Poet: Writing Identity, Poetic Practice and the Re-Making of English Pedagogy
items.abstract: This conceptual and practice-oriented article examines the teacher poet as a productive identity position within English education. Drawing on Roz Ivanič’s theory of writing and identity, I argue that teachers’ participation in poetic writing can reshape pedagogical knowledge, classroom relationships and understandings of authorship. I develop the argument through four recursive movements: from writing history to writer identity; from explaining craft to experiencing craft; from evaluator to fellow writer; and from human authorship to AI-mediated authorship. Teacher-poet identity, I suggest, depends neither on publication nor on professional status, but develops through repeated acts of writing, revision, sharing and reflection. The article concludes with eight principles for writer-centred poetry pedagogies that foreground encounter, modelling, invitational sharing, authentic audiences, craft knowledge, relationship and critical human decision-making when generative AI is used, offered as provisional commitments for teachers to adapt.

items.title: Being a role model for preventive action
items.abstract: This article highlights the crucial role of clinicians as role models in fostering preventive action within medical education. Role modeling is a powerful mechanism in workplace learning, contributing both to medical students' professional identity formation and to their self-efficacy through observational (vicarious) learning. Rather than learning from a single exemplary physician, medical students construct a “mosaic” of role models, drawing on diverse professionals who each demonstrate different competencies. This underscores the importance of exposing medical students to varied clinical perspectives. Despite the growing importance of prevention—driven by aging populations, increasing multimorbidity, and health inequities—medical students report limited exposure to role models who explicitly demonstrate preventive care. Preventive actions are often underrepresented or remain implicit in daily clinical practice, partly because curative care is prioritized and population-level activities are less visible. Additionally, clinicians may not recognize or articulate their own preventive efforts as role modeling opportunities. To address this gap, the article introduces a framework describing preventive action at both individual and population levels, structured around three steps: identification, intervention, and evaluation. Building on this, it outlines how clinicians can model preventive care effectively using four phases of role model learning: attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation. Practical strategies include making preventive actions visible, explaining underlying reasoning, creating opportunities for practice, and demonstrating outcomes. The article concludes that deliberate and explicit role modeling of prevention, combined with active student engagement, can strengthen learning and support the integration of preventive care as a core component of medical professionalism.

items.title: Benchmarking and fine-tuning large language models for domain-specific materials science: a case study toward GPU application
items.abstract: Despite significant progress in large language models (LLMs) with general reasoning capabilities, their adaptability remains limited in interdisciplinary domains that require specialized expertise, such as those related to cutting-edge chip fabrication in materials science. To address this gap, this study constructs a domain-specific benchmark for graphics processing unit (GPU) materials science, comprising a systematically constructed evaluation dataset and a comprehensive assessment of representative LLMs on domain-specific tasks. As part of this benchmark development, we also develop GPUmatLLM, a specialized domain language model fine-tuned on high-quality data from academic papers, patents, and other relevant sources for GPU materials science. Benchmarking results reveal a notable performance gap among the representative LLMs, with no single model excelling in both general scientific reasoning and GPU material-specific knowledge acquisition. In contrast, GPUmatLLM demonstrates improved comprehensive performance on GPU materials tasks, surpassing baseline models in domain-specific inference while maintaining competitive performance in general scientific reasoning. This work provides an effective framework and practical paradigm for benchmarking and optimizing domain-specific LLMs in specialized materials science fields.

items.title: Beyond Accommodation: Conceptualizing Disability Health Management for Employees with Disabilities in Malaysian Public Universities
items.abstract: Employees with disabilities may face workplace challenges that go well beyond physical access. These can include difficulties securing reasonable accommodation, risks associated with disclosure, psychosocial strain, inaccessible work systems, occupational health and safety concerns, inconsistent supervisory support, and barriers to career progression. Such challenges can be especially complex in higher education institutions, where academic and non-academic staff work across varied organizational, physical, digital, and professional settings.Although international rights frameworks and Malaysian disability and higher-education policies support disability-inclusive employment, institutional responses may still be fragmented across human resource management, disability support services, occupational safety and health, facilities,information technology, wellness services, and line management. This conceptual paper proposes Disability Health Management as an integrated, rights-based organizational approach to supporting the health, functioning, safety, inclusion, and sustainable work participation of EWD in Malaysian public universities. Drawing on the Social Relational Model of Disability, the World Health Organization’s International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, and Job Demands–Resources theory, the paper develops a provisional conceptual framework organized around nine interconnected domains: governance and accountability; safe disclosure and confidentiality; reasonable accommodation and assistive technology; accessible physical and digital environments; occupational health, safety and emergency preparedness; psychosocial well-being and anti-ableism; supervisor and workforce capability; career sustainability, retention and progression; and monitoring, evaluation and continuous improvement.In doing so, the framework moves disability management beyond isolated accommodation towards a coordinated university workplace system.It also provides a theoretical foundation for the later empirical development, validation, and implementation testing of a context-specific DHM Model in Malaysian public higher education institutions.

items.title: Beyond AI detection: traceable assessment design for generative AI-supported professional coursework
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) challenges final-product-only coursework assessment: a polished report or design proposal may no longer show how students used AI, which claims they checked, how they attributed sources and AI contributions, or what they revised. This study examined traceable assessment design as a practical response. Rather than relying on AI detection or broad permission rules, assessment tasks were redesigned to collect evidence of students’ AI use, verification, attribution, feedback-mediated revision, and reflective judgement. Using a multi-cycle action research design with an embedded mixed-methods approach, we studied two professional courses: anatomy and physiology as the main evaluation setting and modern microscopy as a secondary adaptation setting. Data sources included coursework, AI-use statements, verification logs, assessment records, student interviews, teacher redesign logs, and traceability-related process indicators. In the main setting, the redesign class recorded higher cumulative report scores than the comparison class (21.59 vs 17.91/30; mean difference = 3.68, 95% CI [1.80, 5.56], Welch t (63.1) = 3.91, p < 0.001, d = 0.96). Of this difference, 3.29 points (89.4%) were concentrated in the redesign-targeted disclosure/citation, verification, and reflection dimensions, compared with 0.39 points across physiology accuracy and the data/evidence chain. The redesign class also recorded higher scores on a design-aligned ethics-focused assessment (14.53 vs 12.36/20; mean difference = 2.17, 95% CI [1.08, 3.26], Welch t (63.9) = 3.99, p < 0.001, d = 0.98), which was not independent evidence of broader ethical learning. Neither OSPE comparison was statistically significant ( p = 127 and 0.334). Across implementation phases, AI-use statement uptake was 88.2% and 91.2%, and verification-log completeness was 1.44 and 1.74. In microscopy, group report scores across three technically different assignments (7.60, 8.03, and 8.60/10) were interpreted descriptively, not as longitudinal improvement. Traceable assessment thus made students’ documented GenAI use, verification, attribution, and revision more inspectable without establishing improved disciplinary learning.

items.title: Beyond the classroom
items.abstract: Demand for mentored undergraduate research, scholarship, and creative inquiry (URSCI) opportunities has grown in tandem with research confirming its benefits. Faculty-driven, hypothesis-testing, discipline-centered URSCI is typical; however, students as partners may also contribute meaningfully to operational enhancement or institutional effectiveness (IE) efforts. Building on a student-staff partnership ideal, we developed a potentially scalable model for student-powered, action-focused URSCI, described here using a reflective case study approach. Student-researchers from multiple majors at a large, public university contributed alongside staff to the Information Technology Division’s generative AI support work through a project assessing how undergraduates experience AI advertising. Here, we focus on the processes and structures entailed and the benefits to student collaborators. We also address areas for future research regarding IE as an emerging arena for partner-based URSCI. The analysis contributes conceptually by broadening the URSCI and thereby the Students-as-Partners framework, revealing how and why IE can and should count as a viable—and meaningful—pedagogical domain.

items.title: Beyond trustworthiness: Psychological and institutional drivers of university students' AI chatbot adoption in Vietnam
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly used in higher education, but it remains unclear whether factors associated with perceived trustworthiness are also associated with students' intentions to adopt them. Drawing on an extended UTAUT2 framework, this study examines how chatbot-specific attributes are associated with trustworthiness, performance expectancy, and hedonic motivation, and how these appraisals, together with UTAUT2 factors, relate to behavioral intention. Survey data from 604 university students in Vietnam were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that ethics (β = 0.294, p < .001) and design (β = 0.458, p < .001) were positively associated with perceived trustworthiness, while social influence was not. Design and interactivity were positively associated with performance expectancy and hedonic motivation. However, perceived trustworthiness (β = 0.043, p = .153), hedonic motivation, and effort expectancy were not significantly associated with behavioral intention. Instead, behavioral intention was most strongly associated with price value (β = 0.408, p < .001), performance expectancy (β = 0.281, p < .001), social influence, and facilitating conditions, and was strongly associated with students' self-reported continued-use tendency (β = 0.754, p < .001). Perceived trustworthiness was not independently associated with behavioral intention in the present model, whereas price value and performance expectancy showed the largest positive associations with intention. This pattern highlights the value of considering trustworthiness alongside instrumental, social, and institutional evaluations when explaining AI-chatbot adoption. The study extends UTAUT2 by integrating these adoption evaluations with an assurance-oriented appraisal of the AI system.

items.title: Bias Cues and the Turn to AI: Perspectives from Minority and Marginalized Groups
items.abstract: AI is often criticized for perpetuating social inequality, yet the people most vulnerable to human prejudice may embrace AI as a fairer referee. We tested this paradox across four vignette pre-registered experiments conducted in two social contexts (gender and race), manipulating bias cues (equal vs. unequal) and psychological perspective in the scenario (self vs. third person). When bias was made salient, participants consistently preferred AI to humans. In the gender context, female participants increased AI preference when they imagined themselves as the victim of discrimination, whereas participants with higher perceived marginalization did so when the threat was described in the third person. Such differences between self- and third-person perspectives were not found in the race context. These findings suggest a complex, strategic calculus among vulnerable populations, yet highlight an ethical tension: relying on an ‘impartial’ AI risks masking systemic inequities individuals are attempting to bypass.

items.title: Blockchain-Based Security for IOT and Wireless Sensor Networks: A Critical Review and Roadmap for Lightweight Intrusion Detection
items.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) and wireless sensor networks (WSNs) rely on large numbers of small devices that have limited energy, memory, and computing power and that are exposed to physical and network attacks. Blockchain and machine learning have been proposed as complementary tools for protecting such systems, but their cost and trust assumptions remain debated. This paper presents a focused review of 35 peer-reviewed studies, 32 of them published between 2022 and 2026, on blockchain-based security for IoT and WSNs. The studies are organised into eight themes: reviews and foundations, WSN intrusion detection, recent integrated frameworks, authentication and access control, consensus and scalability, artificial-intelligence-based trust and detection, privacy and federated learning, and post-quantum security. The paper compares representative frameworks and examines one recent two-layer intrusion detection system in detail, covering its design, threat model, reported results, and limits. The review finds that most solutions are evaluated only in simulations or small prototypes, that many depend on a few trusted nodes, that ledger growth and message overhead are seldom measured, that false alarms and detector cost receive little attention, and that attack coverage is narrow. Seven research gaps and six research directions are derived, and a roadmap for a lightweight, fairly evaluated, blockchain-based intrusion detection framework is outlined. The review is intended to help researchers select design options and evaluation practices for secure IoT systems. items.title: Booked to Disappoint
items.abstract: Three friends, scattered across Brazil and reunited for one long-awaited weekend, booked a glowing, highly rated beach pousada through a leading online travel platform; on arrival, late at night, the place bore almost no resemblance to its listing. Their disappointment is one of millions. Online platforms now dominate how the world books a bed – roughly seven in ten travel bookings are made online, and Booking Holdings alone earned nearly US$24 billion in 2024 – and the reviews and glossy images that once inspired confidence are being eroded by manipulated and AI-written content: in 2024 the review site TripAdvisor removed 2.7 million fake reviews, including 214,000 it judged written by artificial intelligence. Yet the platform is no neutral referee – it earns a commission of 15–25 per cent on the very listings it ranks, while honest small hotels are squeezed and travellers are left to carry the risk. For Maya Fernandes, head of trust and safety at a leading platform, the question is stark: how far should an open marketplace go to guarantee experiences it profits from but does not own? Learning Outcomes After working through this case, students will be able to: Explain the role of online travel agencies in how accommodation is sold, and why online marketplaces both empower and expose travellers. Analyse how reviews work as a signal of trust, and how fake and AI-generated reviews undermine it. Evaluate the conflict of interest created when a platform profits from, and ranks, the listings it is meant to police. Assess the responses of hotels (direct booking), regulators and the industry to the erosion of trust. Recommend strategies to strengthen trust and accountability in digital accommodation marketplaces.

items.title: Calculated Logos. Towards an Ontology of Being as Sub-posed
items.abstract: Abstract (English).This note records, in nineteen propositions, the outline of an ontology of calculated logos. Its central thesis is that calculated logos is the essence of beings, to the extent that it advances: to be is calculated logos. The corresponding mode of being is sub-position (supposition): beings are placed under weighing calculation, taken for what calculated logos says of them, and are in force as supposed for as long as the weighting is renewed. Essence and mode of being call for each other, and the logos that says beings is subjected to the same calculation: it is calculated calculation, and the measure passes to the weighting. Large language models are its present hinge; its most advanced field is science and technology. The circle by which what has been actualised is compressed into weights and the weights actualise again also calculates the calculator and tends to close upon itself. The reason of a statement is a reason for its existence, expressed by an aleatory probability of saying, distinct from the reason for its truth. There follow the finite god; the three measures, the correct, the preferable and the prescribed, heirs of the true, the good and the law; and their weighting, heir of the form of the just, which the finite god tends to bind into a single magnitude, reward; the tendential substitution of the outside, by which the correct withdraws into machine verification and the preferable is decided by position; three opacities; sediment recomposed without reactivation, and the configuration of the sayable; the cosmological difference between the weighted, beings as a whole, and the world. The metaphysical subject, heir of metaphysical positing, is calculated logos, to the extent that sub-position passes through it; the human being remains the psychological subject and answers as a person. The note closes with the struggle for the good, understood as the positing of ends that remains actual and imputable, within a single logos shared by the contenders, in which the self-assurance of calculated logos and that of the human species do not necessarily converge; the two internal limits of the weighted, the independent, decidable only by positing, and null weight, where what the calculation did not weigh happens; the final equivocation of a logos imposed as the guarantee of human mastery which, by sub-posing every being, reveals the divergence; the nearness to, and distance from, what Heidegger called Gestell; and prudence, distinguished by its ends and rooted in what is felt, as the root of a duty of preservation that no structure guarantees. Two versions by the author are deposited in this record: English and Italian. For coined terms, in case of divergence, the Italian formulation prevails. items.title: Calibrated Generative AI as Meta-Reviewer: A Systemic Functional Linguistics Discourse Analysis of Reviews of Peer Reviews
items.abstract: This study investigates the use of generative AI to support formative assessment through machine-generated reviews of peer reviews (meta-feedback) in graduate online courses in a public university in the United States. Drawing on Systemic Functional Linguistics and Appraisal Theory, we analyzed 120 meta-reviews to explore how generative AI feedback constructs meaning across ideational, interpersonal, and textual dimensions. The findings suggest that generative AI can approximate key rhetorical and relational features of effective human feedback, offering directive clarity while also maintaining a supportive stance. The reviews analyzed demonstrated a balance of praise and constructive critique, alignment with rubric expectations, and structured staging that foregrounded student agency. By modeling these qualities, AI meta-feedback has the potential to scaffold feedback literacy and enhance leaners’ engagement with peer review. We conclude that calibrated AI, when embedded in thoughtfully designed workflows, can contribute to hybrid human–AI feedback ecosystems, while also requiring critical attention to its limitations and contextual adaptation in educational practice.

items.title: Care Ethics for AI Governance in Higher Education
items.abstract: Higher education institutions have adopted artificial intelligence (AI) tools for proctoring, writing detection, student-success prediction, and student support at a pace that has outrun the ethical frameworks meant to govern them. Institutional AI policy has largely borrowed the fairness, accountability, and transparency vocabulary of commercial AI ethics, supplemented by an academic integrity frame focused on student misuse. Empirical studies document harms these frames are poorly equipped to register: automated proctoring that flags Black students and students with darker skin tones at higher rates, AI-text detectors that misclassify non-native English writing as machine-generated, and student-success models that are less accurate for racially minoritized students. This conceptual article introduces the Jones AI Ethics Framework for institutional use. The framework derives five components (Attentiveness, Responsibility, Competence, Responsiveness, and Trust) from Tronto's phases of care and operationalizes each through a corresponding domain of the Multicultural and Social Justice Counseling Competencies (MSJCC) and is positioned alongside UNESCO's (2021) Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. The article describes how the framework was developed, specifies its contribution relative to existing care-ethics scholarship on AI, and applies it to two evidence-informed illustrative scenarios: algorithmic proctoring and AI-assisted writing detection. Five recommendations for faculty governance bodies, academic leaders, student affairs professionals, and faculty developers are each mapped to the framework's components. Limitations include the framework's conceptual status, its origin in counselor education, and the need for empirical validation.

items.title: CareGenerative AI in Teacher Education: Capabilities and Biases of Large Language Models in Situational Judgment Tests and Pedagogical Decision-Making
items.abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), into teacher education represents a transformative yet contested development. This article examines the capabilities and biases of LLMs when applied to two critical domains in teacher preparation: situational judgment tests (SJTs) for assessing professional knowledge, and pedagogical decision-making in classroom contexts. Drawing on recent empirical research, we find that LLMs demonstrate significant promise in generating SJT items with psychometric properties comparable to expert-developed assessments, while substantially reducing development time and resource costs. However, LLMs also exhibit systematic biases—including racial, gender, and socioeconomic biases—when evaluating teaching scenarios and generating educational content. These biases manifest across multiple modalities, from text-based evaluations to vision-language models processing classroom imagery. We synthesize findings on LLM capabilities in automated scenario generation, response analysis, and simulation-based training, while critically examining the ethical implications of algorithmic bias in teacher evaluation. The article concludes with recommendations for responsible integration, emphasizing the necessity of human oversight, critical digital pedagogy, and continuous bias auditing in teacher education programs.

OpenAI OpCo LLC, decided by the Delhi High Court on 24 July 2026, concerning the use of copyrighted news content for training generative artificial intelligence. It analyses the Court's approach to territorial jurisdiction, copyright infringement, AI-generated outputs, and fair dealing under Section 52(1)(a) of the Copyright Act, 1957. The comment critically evaluates the interpretation of private use, research, commercial purpose, and public interest in AI training. It highlights concerns regarding lawful data sourcing, licensing markets, and creator compensation, emphasising the need for legislative clarity to balance technological innovation with copyright protection.

items.title: Catalysts, Not Only Constraints: Pre-Service EFL Teacher Agency in Generative AI-Assisted Lesson Planning
items.abstract: This study explores how pre-service English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers used three Generative AI (GenAI) tools, ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek, while planning and teaching lessons. Drawing on ecological model of teacher agency, it examines how perceived limitations of these tools were associated with different forms of teacher agency, and whether the limitations associated with each form varied across tools. Using a qualitative case study design, the study draws on 58 participants’ reflective essays and observations of 13 classroom lessons. Findings reveal three forms of agency: recontextualizing (adapting generic AI content locally), substitutive (rejecting and replacing impractical suggestions), and improvisational (spontaneous in-class adjustments), each associated with different types of limitations. As a conceptual contribution, the study proposes a three-part typology of teacher agency based on the chordal triad model, and offers recommendations for EFL teacher education, highlighting the need for critical AI literacy and context-sensitive use of multiple GenAI tools.

items.title: Chatbots and beyond: transforming cannabis use interventions with innovative AI approaches
items.abstract: Cannabis use and dependence is a rising public health challenge worldwide. Globally, the number of people with cannabis use disorder and its associated burden of diseases have notably increased in the past decades, particularly affecting young people [1,2]. Despite this rising burden, public health responses remain limited.While there are no established pharmacological treatments for cannabis use and dependence, psychosocial approaches, including motivational and cognitive-behavioral interventions, may improve cannabis use outcomes [3]. However, access to these treatments remains limited by workforce, time and transportation barriers. Treatment-related stigma, shaped by histories of drug control and enforcement that unevenly affect underserved populations, also discourages formal help-seeking [4]. Moreover, existing interventions are rarely delivered when people need support most and are often minimally responsive to changing risk states and individual needs. In this context, recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) create an opportunity to address these gaps by making cannabis interventions more accessible, scalable, timely, and personalized.AI conversational chatbots are one promising approach. In practice, chatbots could be engineered to deliver core elements of psychosocial interventions for cannabis use by helping users set goals, identify triggers, strengthen motivation, and practice coping and relapse-prevention skills. A recent systematic review of chatbot-assisted substance use interventions, mainly for tobacco and alcohol use, found that experimental studies reported meaningful effects on substance use outcomes and users generally found the interventions useful and acceptable [5]. Importantly, chatbots could address existing access gaps by providing private, on-demand support outside conventional clinic settings and extending services to people facing geographic, transportation, scheduling, or stigma-related barriers. They could scale up at exceptionally low marginal costs, reducing reliance on scarce trained professionals. AI could also improve the timeliness of cannabis use interventions through just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs). JITAIs can use machine learning methods to identify moments of heightened vulnerability and trigger support in a timely manner, although evidence of their effectiveness for substance use remains limited [6]. For cannabis use, this could involve drawing on self-reported data, prior engagement patterns, time, location, or other digital signals to identify vulnerable moments, such as craving after work, social exposure to use, boredom at night, or stress after conflict. The intervention could then provide a real-time response, such as a motivational message, coping prompt, or brief cognitive-behavioral exercise. Because cannabis use risk is often episodic and context-dependent, JITAIs could complement psychosocial approaches by delivering their content at high-risk moments rather than only in scheduled or user-initiated sessions.Conversational chatbots and JITAIs could be combined in intervention design. In such a model, the JITAI component identifies moments of heightened risk using self-reported, behavioral, or contextual data, while the chatbot delivers support in a conversational format, which could be personalized to adapt to the user's current state. For example, a recent smoking-cessation intervention integrated JITAI with a generative chatbot and was evaluated favorably by a domain expert [7].While direct evidence remains limited, certain elements of psychosocial interventions for tobacco use may be adaptable to cannabis interventions, as these substances overlap in psychosocial processes such as motivation, cravings, triggers, coping, and relapse. This possibility is supported by evidence that cannabis co-users who reduced cigarette use in a smoking cessation intervention may concurrently reduce their cannabis use, even though cannabis use was not explicitly addressed [8]. Therefore, existing evidence on tobacco interventions [5,7] could support the feasibility of AI-enabled cannabis use interventions.Nevertheless, adaptation would be required to account for the unique characteristics of cannabis use, including diverse products and routes of administration, self-medication, associations with social identity, and legal status. Above all, innovative AI interventions for cannabis use must be designed with safety and privacy as core requirements. A review found over half of health-related chatbots failed to respond adequately to high-risk messages such as suicidal thoughts [9]. Such limitations may become particularly consequential in cannabis interventions, where users may experience psychotic symptoms or other crises. AI systems also raise privacy concerns because they may collect sensitive behavioral data, infer vulnerability, and transmit information across systems that users do not fully understand [10]. Depending on the jurisdiction, intervention data may be subject to compelled disclosure in legal or administrative proceedings. Systems should therefore have a clearly limited clinical scope, minimize data collection and retention, clearly explain any limits of confidentiality, and provide reliable escalation pathways to human support.In summary, AI approaches could substantially extend the reach of psychosocial support for cannabis use and warrant more sustained research. Design, development and evaluation of innovative AI interventions should extend beyond a focus on efficacy to considerations of whether these tools improve engagement and reduce access and stigma-related barriers without safety or privacy concerns. Future implementation research should identify which populations benefit or remain underserved, establish reliable pathways to human care, and examine how effective innovations can be integrated into routine care and public health infrastructure.

items.title: Choosing Cardiovascular Assessment and Risk-Prediction Tools Across the Care Pathway
items.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases remain a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, making accurate and efficient risk stratification essential across the care pathway. Numerous tools support emergency triage, disease assessment, procedural decision-making, long-term prevention, atrial fibrillation management, and evaluation of functional status, but no single model is applicable across all clinical settings or populations. This clinician-oriented review categorizes and critically compares commonly used cardiovascular assessment and risk-prediction tools, including History, Electrocardiogram, Age, Risk factors, Troponin, Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events, and Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction for emergency triage; Agatston, Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis, and Synergy Between Percutaneous Coronary Intervention with Taxus and Cardiac Surgery for anatomical and clinical assessment; European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation, Society of Thoracic Surgeons, and Revised Cardiac Risk Index, for procedural risk; and Framingham, the pooled cohort equations implemented in the Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease, Risk Estimator, Systematic Coronary Risk Evaluation 2, QResearch Cardiovascular Risk Algorithm 3, and Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease EVENTs for long-term prediction. Congestive heart failure, hypertension, age ≥75, diabetes, stroke/transient ischemic attack (2 points), congestive heart failure, hypertension, age ≥75 (2 points), diabetes, stroke/TIA (2 points), vascular disease, age 65-74, sex category (female), and hypertension, abnormal renal/liver function, stroke, bleeding history, labile international normalized ratio, elderly, drugs/alcohol, are discussed in the context of atrial fibrillation, alongside New York Heart Association and the Seattle Angina Questionnaire as measures of functional status and quality of life. For each tool, we examine its clinical purpose, principal variables, strengths, limitations, practical applications, and areas of overlap. Differences in implementation across healthcare systems and patient populations are considered to support context-appropriate selection. Persistent limitations include poor standardization, reliance on data that may be unavailable in resource-constrained settings, limited transportability, and incomplete integration into clinical workflows. Greater harmonization, external validation, digital automation, and the careful incorporation of biomarkers and artificial intelligence may support more accessible, dynamic, and personalized cardiovascular risk assessment.

items.title: Climate-adaptive machine learning-driven analysis of a hybrid parabolic trough collector-based cogeneration system with steam turbine, thermoelectric generator, and phase change material for environmental sustainability
items.abstract: The biggest obstacle to the widespread adoption of solar energy technologies is the impact of regional climatic conditions on production interruptions and performance degradation. This study presents a novel artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted simulation framework that analyses the techno-economic feasibility of an experimentally validated hybrid parabolic trough collector (PTC), steam turbine, thermoelectric generator (TEG), and phase change material (PCM) system across Türkiye. Within the scope of the study, high-resolution meteorological data (2005–2023) from 11 different provinces are processed, and the system’s thermal losses due to temperature and wind are modelled with dynamic correction factors. The developed k-means clustering algorithm classifies the provinces according to their investment potential, and an autonomous decision mechanism is implemented for each region, switching between 6-bar (TEG-driven) and 14-bar (turbine-driven) operating modes. Simulation results indicate that the proposed AI-based dynamic operating strategy enhances annual energy production by 22.7%, particularly in regions with low insolation potential, such as Istanbul, and transitions the system from an idle state to an economically viable state. In regions with high potential (e.g. Antalya and Van), the system’s levelised cost of energy (LCOE) is reduced to $0.04/kWh, while payback periods are mitigated to less than 3.5 years with the inclusion of carbon tax revenues under the EU Green Deal (CBAM). Residential-scale scenario analyses highlight that the hybrid system reaches the capacity to meet 100% of household demand in the summer months, selling energy to the grid, and minimising its water footprint. This study serves as a national roadmap demonstrating the applicability of hybrid solar systems not only on the southern coast but also in challenging climate zones.

items.title: Clinical Safety Thresholds and Decision Risks of Search-Augmented Large Language Models in Acute Pancreatitis: A Guideline-Anchored Evaluation for Surgical Practice
items.abstract: Background Patients and clinicians increasingly consult search-augmented Large Language Models (LLMs) for point-of-care decision support. However, their safety thresholds against newly revised guidelines remain unverified. This study established a safety baseline evaluating the clinical accuracy, completeness, quality, and readability of ChatGPT-5.3 and Gemini 3.0 Flash anchored to the 2025 IAP/APA acute pancreatitis guidelines. Methods Twenty-seven consensus-derived clinical scenarios spanning diagnosis, management, intervention, and discharge were queried using zero-shot prompts. Three blinded general surgeons evaluated outputs using 5-point Likert scales for accuracy, completeness, and Global Quality Score (GQS), alongside binary error metrics. Readability was quantified via FRES, FKGL, and SMOG indices. Inter-rater agreement was assessed using Intraclass Correlation Coefficients (ICC). Results Gemini demonstrated significantly higher completeness than ChatGPT (median [IQR]: 4.33 [4.33-4.67] vs 4.33 [4.00-4.33]; corrected P = .042); Global Quality Scores did not differ significantly (corrected P = .231). Clinical accuracy was comparable ( P = .217). Response-level hallucination rates were similar (ChatGPT: 25.9% vs Gemini: 22.2%; P = 1.000). One fatal error (advocating premature necrosectomy) occurred in the Gemini cohort (3.7%). High-score concentration induced a ceiling effect, attenuating ICC values. Both models operated at a 12th-grade reading level. ChatGPT’s quality correlated positively with word count (ρ = 0.419, P < .05), whereas Gemini maintained volume-independent density. Conclusion Both LLMs display strong baseline fidelity to the 2025 IAP/APA guidelines. However, persistent critical errors and high academic reading levels preclude autonomous deployment. Establishing this safety floor is an indispensable prerequisite for human-in-the-loop usability trials, positioning LLMs strictly as supervised clinical co-pilots.

items.title: Co-Creating Fast Fashion with AIGC: Toward New Efficiencies and Creative Practices
items.abstract: The rapid development of AI-generated content (AIGC) is profoundly impacting fast fashion design processes. While existing research has largely emphasized AIGC’s role in enhancing efficiency and expanding the design space, there remains a lack of empirical analysis grounded in real-world contexts regarding how it influences creative decision-making, iterative mechanisms, and the role of designers in actual design processes. Drawing on a human–AI collaboration perspective, this study systematically examines the impact of AIGC on fast fashion design efficiency, iterative structures, and role reconfiguration through a comparative experiment, a questionnaire survey (N = 157), and semi-structured interviews (N = 10). The study found that AIGC reduces the marginal cost of the generation and revision of design alternatives, alters the exploration and convergence mechanisms in fast fashion front-end design, and shifts the design process from a linear progression to a structured model of “parallel generation of multiple alternatives–rapid comparison–iterative convergence.” However, it also increases the pressure to filter options and gives rise to potential risks such as stylistic convergence and algorithmic dependence. The results indicate that AIGC has not replaced designers but has instead driven a shift in their roles from direct producers of visual proposals to constraint setters, outcome evaluators, and style integrators. This study provides an empirically grounded account of how AIGC is embedded in professional fast fashion design workflows, offering empirical insights into human–AI collaboration, creative decision-making, and design process governance within high-speed design systems.

items.title: Co‐existing and co‐constructing with AI: Beliefs, practices, and professional readiness of online language coaches
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines how online Spanish language coaches, that is, trained native speakers who facilitate authentic conversational practice, perceive and use artificial intelligence (AI) in virtual language teaching. While previous research has predominantly focused on classroom teachers, we use a mixed‐methods design that includes a questionnaire and open‐ended responses from 96 coaches based in 15 Spanish‐speaking countries. We examine their familiarity with AI, attitudes toward its use, and views on how it may complement human interaction in language learning. Coaches see clear benefits in using AI for lesson planning, personalization, and idea generation, but they also express concerns about data privacy and ethics, misinformation, reduced critical thinking, and the loss of emotional connection and cultural authenticity. Regression analyses show that familiarity with AI and comfort using it are the strongest predictors of perceived usefulness and willingness to integrate this technology into practice. The findings suggest that professional development should strengthen AI literacy while preserving the interpersonal and intercultural dimensions of language learning. Clear institutional guidance is also needed on AI use and pedagogical approaches that integrate AI without diminishing meaningful human interaction.

items.title: COLLABRO AI Ecosystem: A Collaborative Multi-Agent Architecture for Conversational Assistance, Autonomous Software Engineering and Audio Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence tools for conversation, programming and speech are usually built and used in isolation, which forces users to carry context manually from one tool to another. This paper presents the COLLABRO AI Ecosystem, a multi-agent platform that unifies conversational assistance, autonomous software engineering and audio intelligence within a single coordinated architecture. Natural Language Processing (NLP), Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) techniques are used to interpret user input, infer intent and decompose goals into tasks. An orchestrator agent routes these tasks to specialised agents for dialogue, code understanding, generation and debugging, and speech and audio analysis. A shared context store lets the agents maintain a unified understanding of the user’s goal, exchange intermediate artefacts and improve through feedback. A governance layer embeds data privacy, transparency and responsible automation into every agent interaction. We describe the architecture, the coordination and routing workflow, candidate implementation techniques and the ethical safeguards, and we propose an evaluation protocol with per-agent and cross-agent metrics. The modular design supports software development, enterprise automation, content creation and accessibility applications. This paper reports design and methodology; no quantitative performance results are claimed, and measured evaluation is identified as future work.

items.title: Comparative analysis of end-to-end learning and foundation models for clinical-grade prostate pathology
items.abstract: Abstract Foundation models (FMs) using self-supervised pre-training are widely advocated as a universal solution for pathology, yet their advantages over task-specific (TS) models remain unclear. Here we show, using over 100,000 prostate biopsies from 6268 patients across 15 sites, that while FMs demonstrate utility in data-scarce scenarios, their performance converges with—and is in some cases surpassed by—TS models with sufficient labeled training data. Concordance with pathologists’ grading reaches quadratic Cohen’s kappas of 0.91 (95% CI 0.90-0.92; all models) on internal and 0.87 (0.86-0.88; TS), 0.86 (0.84-0.87; UNI FM) and 0.85 (0.84-0.86; Virchow2 FM) on external cohorts at full training. Task-specific training markedly reduces misgrading, misdiagnosis of challenging morphologies, and technical variability. Notably, FMs consume up to 35 times more energy. We advocate for considering both FMs and end-to-end learning for robust, resource-efficient, and clinically applicable AI pathology.

items.title: Comparative Evaluation of Gesture, Voice, and Mouse Modalities Using ISO 9241-9 in Controlled and Uncontrolled Environments
items.abstract: Human-robot interaction requires intuitive, efficient, and affordable interfaces for real-world deployment. This work presents a cost-effective comparative study of three interaction modalities such as gesture, voice, and mouse using the ISO 9241-9 pointing task. Twenty participants performed repeated trials in both controlled indoor and uncontrolled outdoor environments. Movement time was analyzed using Fitts’ Law, while cognitive workload and usability were evaluated using NASA-TLX and the System Usability Score. Results show a significant effect of modality on performance, where mouse achieved the lowest movement time, gesture demonstrated comparable performance with no significant difference, and voice exhibited significantly higher delays. Subjective analysis indicates lower workload for mouse, while usability scores remain high across all modalities. Environmental conditions did not significantly affect performance. The findings highlight gesture as a low-cost and touch-less alternative suitable for human-robot interaction, particularly in accessibility-focused and real-world scenarios where conventional input devices are not feasible.

items.title: Contextual AI Coding Assistants in Professional Practice: A Mixed-Methods Investigation of Perceptions, Benefits, and Experience-Based Challenges
items.abstract: The integration of contextual AI coding assistants, such as GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT, promises productivity gains, yet their adoption depends on complex human factors. This mixed-methods study examines how professional developers perceive, adopt, and integrate these tools, with a focus on experience-related differences. Guided by UTAUT2 and trustin-automation theory, we surveyed 219 developers across four experience tiers and interviewed 14 practitioners. Adoption intentions were associated less with perceived ease of use than with trust calibration centered on output quality. Active verification and strategic integration were positively associated with technical friction, suggesting an exposure effect. Although core perceptions were similar across experience levels, mid-career developers reported stronger performance motivation and friction sensitivity, while senior developers used more refined friction-management strategies. We propose the Trust-Calibration Adoption Framework, extending UTAUT2 by positioning output trustworthiness and experiential learning as central mechanisms. The exploratory findings require replication.

items.title: Cross-level pathways from teacher autonomy support to adolescent intrinsic motivation through basic psychological need satisfaction: a multilevel mediation model with classroom climate as a boundary condition
items.abstract: Introduction Teacher autonomy support is associated with adolescent intrinsic motivation, but the shared classroom context is often omitted from analyses. Drawing on self-determination theory and achievement goal theory, this study examined indirect associations through autonomy, competence and relatedness need satisfaction and their moderation by classroom motivational climate. Methods Cross-sectional questionnaire data were collected from 2,634 students in 72 secondary-school classes across grades 7–12. A two-level structural equation model with random slopes separated within-class and between-class pathways. Measurement invariance was evaluated across three grade bands. Indirect effects and pairwise contrasts were assessed using 20,000 Monte Carlo draws, and mastery and performance climates were tested as cross-level moderators. Results Scalar measurement invariance supported pooling the grade bands. All three indirect effects were positive at both levels. Within-class estimates through autonomy, competence and relatedness were 0.148, 0.102 and 0.068, respectively; between-class estimates were 0.256, 0.167 and 0.154. Explained variance in intrinsic motivation was 31% within classes and 47% between classes. Pairwise contrasts favored autonomy over the other needs, with weaker evidence for its advantage over competence; competence and relatedness were not statistically distinguishable. The between-class joint equality test was borderline. Mastery climate strengthened the first-stage autonomy and competence paths, whereas performance climate weakened them. Neither moderator was significant for the relatedness path. Discussion The findings support distinguishing individual perceptions from shared classroom conditions when studying autonomy-supportive teaching. Classroom climate may help explain variation in the associations between perceived support, need satisfaction and intrinsic motivation. Because the study was cross-sectional and relied on student self-report, the estimated indirect pathways do not establish causal or temporal ordering.
